content: Welcome! We got a little treat for you today. Um, myself, the soul fester Mr. Marcellus Williams, and my coach, and actually Marcellus's coach as well, Brad Couliard, we teamed up together and we did a little Q&A. Um, if you follow us on Instagram as well, we put a poll up or a question box to be able to submit questions, and we picked the ones that we really thought would be of the most benefit and maybe we haven't covered before, and really dove into them. Um, and we've got part of it on my channel, the video you're watching right now, and then the other half on Marcellus's. So I'll make sure to link that below and make sure to go watch that if you want the totality of the Q&A. So within that too, um, a lot of you may not be as active on Instagram if you haven't seen. Marcellus, Brad, and I are going to be hosting an event at Corrupted Strength, Russ Orihi's gym, on September 25th. It's a really cool event; it's a seminar. But what we're really trying to do is kind of elevate what a seminar typically is. Seminars are just talking throughout the day, maybe a little technique analysis, but we really want to bring a true experience to the powerlifting community. So, you're going to have me, Brad, and Marcellus, and actually a guest presenter, Derek Kugne, presenting on different topics. I'll be talking about high-frequency benching, Brad's going to be talking about defining good technique, Marcellus will be discussing accessory movement programming within powerlifting, and then Derek will be talking about kind of... The rehab side of things, but within that too, we're going to be having some of the best lifters from across the country coming out. People like Bob Matthews, Ashton Roska, Shawn Norriega, Jasmine Penn, and Gabby Martinez. I mean, the list goes on. I think we have 18 to 19 of some of the best lifters in the country coming out that you can interact with. You will be able to hang out throughout the day. They're going to be doing exhibition events such as the tandem deadlift, which is sponsored by 110 Percent. We've got the bench press for reps, sponsored by A7, and then we have the pause squat for time, sponsored by Squats Apparel. Those pros are going to be competing in those events, putting on a show for everyone. We're going to have a lift the pro. This session is where everyone can lift together at the end of the day. There will be a free catered lunch and a free GBT collab shirt that will be coming with it. We're going to have a Q&A with the pros, and we will also have this live stream. A lot of cool stuff to really create a true experience for the powerlifting fanatic, where not only can you get some great information from coaches, but you can also hang out and experience something that a lot of people aren't typically able to do: getting all of the best lifters together in one area and having a pretty unique experience, being able to interact with them. The cap is set at 60 entries. We're going to have almost 20 pros, but we only have 60 spots. People attending, so registration is still available. It's going to be closing on August 27th, and then we're going to go from there. I'm gonna put the link down in the description box below if you're interested in attending that. Again, it's going to be on September 25th from, I believe, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. at corrupted summit, down in Houston, Texas, and we'd love for you to attend. But otherwise, you're here for the video; you're here for some questions and answers and to get some knowledge. We're talking in this video about it. I think we are talking about ascending sets, discussing some of the biggest unexpected coaching lessons we learned, talking about squat frequency, and some other awesome topics. So, without further ado... Without further ado, here's the Q&A.

All right, Marcellus, how would you go about programming ascending sets? Oh, I’ll make it broad, so I’ll say, give me one—like in what instances or where—like I think we program ascending sets. How to program them? I don't want to say it's simple, but you're sending work. Like, why would you, in what instances, and why would you be programming ascending sets? Got you. Okay, so there are a couple of reasons. One can be if I'm trying to get a client to have a little bit of additional workload, but not so much that I think it's overly fatiguing. Then that’s when I like ascending sets. I'm sure we all have those clients where it's like, you know, they work up to their top set, and the top set goes really well. You give them back down volume after that. Even if it's super sub-max and they're just direct on it, they just don't feel good; they don't perform very well with it. Because after hitting that top set, they don't recover as well for whatever reason. I like using ascending sets in that case. I have a client named Family, for example. On her secondary deadlift day, what we found was whenever she worked up to, you know, like on a primary day, if she hits her top set and then back down, she's fine. But on the secondary day, after she worked up to her top sets, she just kind of gasps by the time she gets those back downs without quite doing the quality we want out of it. So instead, we switched her to ascending sets, you know, in the same sense. Five, six, whatever it may be, up to an assigned RPE. That way, we're kind of getting in a little bit of that additional volume through the ascending sets. But once they hit that higher-end threshold, whatever the exertion is that's separated today, then she's good to go. We kind of get that quality there. So that's one reason that I like to do it. Another one is just sometimes skill practice, really kind of like grooving the pattern a little bit more, helping the lifter learn to gauge their RPEs better. Sometimes the client might say, you know, let's say they have a top set of three or four, but they're just doing singles or doubles to warm up, and they're like, 'Oh, this warm-up felt really good for a single.' Kind of jumped the gun, got aggressive with their next load attempt, and it ends up being overshot. So, having them be like, 'Okay, you have a top set for this RPE. Now you have to do working sets of four for every work until you get there,' kind of helps them get a better gauge for their body and move the moving pad a little bit better as well. I could probably go on for too long about all the reasons, because I think there are so many reasons why to do ascending sets, and I think they're a fantastic tool to add a couple to it. I'll try to ramble them off quick: one, someone who is time-limited; it could be on certain days they're time-limited, but if you're doing ascending sets, that tends to allow them to be able to kind of work up to. Their top set—get it done, get in and out, and quicker. You're talking a little bit about the top set and then not feeling recovered. I see a lot, and I think there are a lot of people who, I don't know if it's recovering; I think it's a lot of times like a mental drain and letdown. They put all of their energy into that top set, and so by doing ascending sets, I can get them to have better quality work, aka a better average intensity of their entire workout, which then increases total stress today. You have some people who just suck at warming up. They don't do anything; they get under the bar, they do 135, they do 225, and then boom, they're ready to do their working sets with 315. And then they say, 'Oh, I felt like crap on my...' Top set, but once I got my working sets or my back downs, they started to feel better. Well, they probably just weren't warming up enough. All right, I'm gonna force him to warm up another way. You said, I already said it for gauging RPE, and yeah, I'm blanking on some others. I could keep going on forever. I'll let Brad go because you probably are thinking of a couple that I haven't said. I mean, I basically use them primarily on secondary days, just in general. Like where I place them, I typically reserve the top set back down approach for primary days, just because of the nature of what competition is like. I like a little bit more of a polarizing effect on that primary day as opposed to like a secondary day. But yes, basically. To dampen output a bit, so you know, if I'm thinking over a structure of like 12 weeks, I might do something like ascending true sets—five, six, seven or six, seven, eight—up until maybe the four-week mark. I might go into something more like a top set approach on that secondary day, just to get a little bit more practice with that concept, as well as still giving a little bit of a polarizing effect for that rep range or that intensity. But I mean, I think you can go for it; it's not necessarily true five, six, seven. You could go five, six, and then drop five to ten percent, whatever. But I think there are a lot of different strategies. Like Steve said, you can go on and on with the combinations. Intensity adjustments and RPE configurations that you want out of it are endless, so it's just a matter of what you're doing. For example, they asked about how do you program them. The obvious one is, let's say we're doing sets of five or we're just going to send up six, seven, eight RPE. It could be descending volume; it could be five, four, three, six, seven, eight. It could be ascending volume where you do three, four, five, six, seven, eight RPE, but it's the same weight every single time. You're just adding a rep each time. There are so many different ways you can actually do ascending sets. I'm really big on doing a top rep set and then doing a single because way too often, people prioritize and put all their energy into their. Single and then their rep work sucks from it. So, a lot of times, I ascend into the single by doing like two or three ascending rep sets, and then ascend into their literal last set of the day, which is their single. You'll find that all of a sudden they can do all these sets magically well, versus if I do the reverse order, their single grows great and everything else goes to crap. So, yeah, there's a lot of ways you can do it. One more thing I will do in there too is I like using, if I increase someone's frequency on a lift—so we go from say three times a week to four times a week—I sometimes like to start with having like an ascending set to kind of gauge what their work capacity is like with that extra bench day, and then from there I can start wanting to. Give them more, like, you know, straight sets, drop backs, et cetera. But I find that it's just not increasing too much too quickly when you do it that way. I'll give one more too, because again, there are so many ways you can do this. You can change the ascending work as you go through a block. You could have four ascending sets in week one, three ascending sets and a back off in week two, two ascending sets and two back offs. You can change and like, or even like, one block is ascending sets and, you know, you're increasing average intensity and stress and masking top-end strength. Then, in the next block, you pull off ascending sets and you do a top set approach model to kind of work on peak strength. I do that a lot with the bench press in particular. Let's push some high stress and high exertion, and average intensity, to kind of create the adaptations. A lot of people can kind of tend to over, I wouldn't say overreach, but like push bench and not get, and not kind of tank from it. Then pull back off of that and go to a top set back-off approach more for care about peak intensity. Then we see kind of the output rates up there. So yeah, we've probably, again, we've all said it, we probably could make a two-hour video on ascending sets because there's so many ways to utilize them.

So, Brad, I'll move on to you. What's the most common frequency you see with each style of competition lift? Um, two to three on the squat, um, one to two on the deadlift, and then bench, I mean, bench has such a wide range, um, but I even... I think that the people who can tolerate lower frequencies overall could still handle about four on average. Typically, it's between three to five; obviously, there are exceptions to the norm of six to seven per week. What's showing up to now? Six seconds? Yeah, okay, so six is towards that top-end range. However, anywhere between three to five is the most comfortable for bench press that I've seen. I'll throw one thing out, and you tell me if you agree or not, because I think we're all going to agree on that. I have an opinion that too many people try to squat three days a week and think it's going to be magical, just like increasing bench press. Increasing bench press frequency is not the same as increasing squat frequency. I think way too many people squat three days a week, and they should not be. I absolutely agree; I agree 100%. Yeah, it's not for the faint of heart at all. It's funny because I found that a lot of my clients get to a point where they're doing better with two days a week, especially as they get stronger. I do have some lifters, right? Like, I can use my client Clare as an example. He's a big squatter, and he has his primary and secondary squat days. We did recently give him a third squat day, but it's like a three by three, and I'm talking like 60%. Yeah, it really helps him feel a better groove for his primary squat day. That's it. But as far as pushing extensively high volume three days a week, I find for most people it's really not necessary. I'm also big on 'less is more'; rebuild less for as long as you can. Oftentimes, for my clients who do have that third squat day, it's something that is just a super sub-max priming day, or it's like a variation like SSB, something of that nature. But I definitely think that way more people would do well on twice a week squatting, and they don't even realize it. Small off-base mess-up to go with the squatting part: you guys could tell me if you've done something different. I still, to this day, don't think I've ever... Programmed the third squat day to be intensive in any way? Yeah, always super sub-max. I think where, again, I'm going to where people are going wrong is they're adding a third squat day, yet they're doing no accessory moves for the lower body. Yep, like there is such low-hanging fruit there. If you had a third squat day, that's more fatigue carryover to deadlifts; like, that's more low back intensity. I mean, low back intensive work. We could be doing belt squats, pendulum, or hack squats or something like that and getting direct leg work. I'm going to say, for the majority of powerlifters, barring they're doing lower body accessory work, they're probably not actually targeting their legs enough because, I mean, it... Borrowing your Connor Borker, even he probably stole his accessory work. And you have super short femurs, or I have Lorenzo. Lorenzo doesn't do a lot of accessory stuff; like, the squat isn't always the best quad builder. It's a great squat builder, but that alone isn't just a great quad builder. It tends to take a little bit more than that. So yeah, you should be, I mean, it could—y'all may have done the strategy too. Maybe the third squat day is belt squats. Yeah, I've done that. I've got a lot of clients who do that, actually. I would even say that logic applies to bench to a certain degree. I have clients, you know, they come to me—maybe they were just benching like two times a week before they came to me. I started three times a week, and things are going somewhere, like, oh should we go to four? And I'm like, let's get you stronger first and then do that. The progress you can make off that is great; you milk that. Then once you get to that point, cool, now you have that fourth day still in your back pocket. Especially with the bench, if you run something for long enough—like you go from three to four days a week—you're running for long enough, it's very, very difficult to go backward from there at that point and make the same progress. So that's what I try to milk what you can for as long as you can. Yep. Yeah, I mean, I absolutely agree with everything you guys are saying. It's, it's, you can do, like, especially for squat, I mean... 3x squat is definitely taxing, especially for someone who came from the traditional DUP model. Being able to handle a 3x8, you know, 4x4 or 3x6, 4x4 every week, with an AMRAP at the end of the week, is not something you can maintain from the standpoint of intensity across the whole week. It definitely needs a bridge, so to speak, like you mentioned, Marcellus, to a 3x3, which is super light, just to kind of bridge the fact that you're squatting four days apart on the main days and secondary primary days. The accessory work—I mean, you can utilize what Steve talked about, which is just utilizing accessory work to support your training. Hypertrophy growth, uh, within the specific isolated tissues, whether that's, you know, a pendulum hack, a belt squat, leg extensions, leg curls, stuff like that, can be fine, right? Because it's just about managing stress across the whole week. So, if you're adding that in there for specific purposes, great! I think that's a great idea for someone who needs a little bit more specificity going into a prep or something like that. But, obviously, other things need to drop out, and you need to be more strategic with accessory work, like Bulgarians or what have you, on where they're placed. So that you are not just tanking everything at that point. Because it is, it is not a... yeah, it's tough. So, a question that was coming up... And I'm just going to start with it now. It wasn't necessarily my question, but it fits into this, so it would be silly to have to come back around to it. What would a three-day-a-week squat layout look like? We're already kind of alluding to it; that third squat day, I think all three of us agree, is not going to be intensive. There are two main things I'm looking at, or three main things. About two is that day needing to be more skill practice-based or more filling a volume gap. Then within that, what does the lifter tend to get beat up more from: volume, like higher rep work, or lower rep work? Because that's going to answer all the questions I want. Usually, if you're doing technique-based stuff, it's going to probably lean towards the... We're looking at the lower end of the replication schemes because we're wanting to have a little bit more skill practice towards maintaining position that's a bit more specific to what we do. Um, but at the same time, maybe you have a lifter that, if you're going to work up to any, like even low RPEs, three sets of three at seventy percent might beat them up compared to doing sets of seven at sixty percent. Um, so there's not a right answer there, but those are the things I'm looking at: technique versus volume, and then how does the lifter respond and recover based on intensity versus volume, which some of that comes back to distance traveled. I think some of that, uh, is sex-related; male versus female. I would say I have more women. Who are doing higher volume tertiary days and more men doing lower rep tertiary days? You both are shaking your heads, so I think we're on the same thing there. That comes a lot back just to distance traveled. I mean, women tend to be shorter; they're handling lower loads, and all that kind of stuff. They usually just tend to need more volume. So that's generally how I'm going to set up the third day. This is going with a question we just had. A lot of times, just sending sets on that, I would say probably eighty to ninety percent of the tertiary squat days I have are assembling sets with clients right now. Yeah, I cap a lot of those days too, to specific intensities that I don't want to crest too high from. I mean, literally, I'll write five or six RP across the whole block. You know, it's not meant to be challenging anyway, but just to kind of touch on the male-female thing, I'd also find that females are just better squatters in general. Men are more hinge dominant and, you know, a little bit more pitched, and it taxes the lower back a lot more. So, they're a lot more sensitive to stuff like that, whereas I think females can handle, I think the females could handle the 3x a lot more comfortably than a male could. Yeah, again, starting point, it's all context at that point. Sorry, yeah, for real. That third day is the same thing. If it's not ascending sets, it's usually just like two to... Three straight sets with assigned load. I don't even have a RPE base oftentimes because I just don't want to risk them saying, 'I'm feeling good on this,' oh, this was an RPE 6. So I just give them assigned loads. As far as variation goes, like Steve said, it just comes down to the individual. What I do find is if, let's say, their primary squat was in their secondary squat, there's a close variant, whether it's secondary comp squats or possible tempo, something like that. I usually let that change be a little bit further in variation, maybe like a high bar or something like that, whereas we're pushing some type of variation on the secondary day, and I have that third day be more kind of specific just to kind of grease the groove. The groove, if you will, whether it's like light tempo squats, possibly even just like tempo squats for higher reps. And yeah, I found that too, as far as females versus males in terms of their ability to recover from squatting three times a week. Of course, there are exceptions to that too. But yeah, and once again, I even get to a point where I ask myself sometimes, like, okay, we've been doing this because it gives them that extra practice or whatever it may be, which is great. But I've gotten away from using that day as just extra volume stimulus because at that point, once again, it's like, okay, I can just put a belt squat here or a hack press, something like that. So that's the big thing too because there are. Some people just need that additional volume stimulus, but I'm always okay asking, can I get that from an accessory first? If for whatever reason I can't and it's just not specific enough for them, then that's when I'll maybe have it be like, okay, like a three by six or like a two by eight with super light loads just to get that additional volume there. Yeah, and the question, too, was asking, we all went—I started by going more towards what the third day looks like. It says, what does a three-day week squat layout look like? The other two days look like a two-day squat workout, and then you're just adding a third day. I don't change anything about those other two days when I add in the third day. Those other two days are the same. Matter what, so um all right, I think we'll do two more questions.

Uh, this one's a little tough one. Marcellus, you might have to think about this. Most unexpected coaching lesson you learned? Wow, most unexpected lesson. I'll lead it off. I don't know if this is the most unexpected because there might be more unexpected ones than this, but something that I'll say, as a beginner coach and now to where I'm at now, that has greatly changed is, I definitely thought coaching elite-level people was different than coaching beginners or like intermediate lifters. I thought like it was entirely different and it must be this, like, this thing that like once you know how to do that, like, it's just so much different. And it's literally... Not different at all, other than the fact that most elite-level lifters tend to be a little bit more dedicated. Like, they're elite for a reason. I think, on the grand scheme of things, they tend to be a little more dedicated and control and track variables, which means what you do for them you can have direct feedback on, if it works or not. Versus, I would say on the more beginner spectrum, you've got people who are more consistent on their training days and skipping workouts on their sleep and nutrition, and all that kind of stuff, to where there are big question marks of, 'Is this even working?' or 'Why is this working?' You're like, 'I have no idea.' Where elite-level lifters, it's some... I almost would say sometimes it's easier to coach them. I don't... I know if you all agree, like, I almost think a lot of times with most of my elite-level people, it's easier to coach them because I know if X, Y, and Z is working, it's for the reasons I think it's working. Or if it's not working, I can understand it; I can figure it out. Versus if you have, I don't want to say all beginners are not as serious, but usually beginners and intermediates tend to not be as consistent and invested to an extent. That's where there's a bit more insistence on getting consistencies on knowing: is it the program, is it my coaching, or is it live variables? I can think of one example, just generalized as a coach. I remember when I first decided this was something I wanted to do; it looked like before I even got into it. Like, years ahead of time, and it's like, wow, this looks like such a cool job. You can, like, you know, work at home; everything's so flexible. You just spend all this time, you can go work out, and like, on your own schedule, and you know, relax. And you know, you're coaching, right? It's such a cool thing! Holy [ __ ]! I feel like, uh, you know, obviously structuring time for, you know, downtime and all that kind of stuff. But as a coach, I feel like I'm constantly wanting success for athletes. And it's like putting that, and like the time, like we were talking about—I don't know if it was before the call or whatever—but like, you know, pulling up the program and looking at their program, looking at their numbers to be able... To talk to them, you know, about what they should do: like, that's the amount of effort and work that we put into our coaching is just so beyond what I thought it was like, I guess, like eight years ago, nine years ago. It's just such a different thought process from that. That's the only thing. It's just the grand scheme of things of how it, you know, got to here was unexpected from what I thought nine years ago. So yeah, I think I've got, I've got, I've got, yeah, I've got a pretty, I got my answer now, kind of. Two, so the first thing I'll say is, and this is more so like if you're a coach, you're also a lifter yourself, it's like, you know, your people, your clients look to you to teach them all these different things and help progress stuff like... That I have made so much progress in my own training by learning things from my clients. In the sense that you try so many different things with them through trial and error, whether that's the worst of them or not, it gives you things to reference for yourself as well. So that was one thing for me that was very unexpected. I look at some of the changes I made in my own training, and I realized, like, oh yeah, I'm doing this because I did this with, say, Bob or Elijah, and it worked well. I think, oh, this makes sense for me. But I think probably a big one is, at least for me, when I first got involved in it, was like—and a lot of people might get kind of mad at this—I'm not by any means saying that you shouldn't go... See a professional therapist, but dude, coaching is so much like being a therapist sometimes. I really didn't understand to the degree of how much someone's lifestyle and life factors are involved with it. At this point, obviously, I know that that's a big part of how my coaching works, but when I first got involved in it, you know, you think it's going to be something simple, like, oh, you give people the program, they're going to follow the program, you're going to teach them technique, and they're going to get stronger. When you start to really get deeper into it, you know your clients better, and the different stuff outside the gym that impacts the training impacts the… Stress levels, and realizing how much you have to really know about that stuff, and be involved in it. Really, I guess it's about experience; how much trust a client really has to have in their coach to maximize everything. Because if your client’s not comfortable talking about certain things, there are going to be so many factors of recovery and variables that you can't even account for if you don't know those different lifestyle stressors going on. So that was definitely something for me where I'm like, I now fully understand the importance of that, and I even kind of preach that from the first consultation. Calling for faith, if you talk about anything, you can relate to things that will... Impact your training. But when I first started, I never thought it would be to that deep level, like as far as the role it can play. All right, since I ended up going first on that one, Marcellus, I'll make you go first on this one to be our last one.

Um, because I already know part of your answer here, because I really like your answer to this one: How do you train a client to use RPE if they consistently overshoot? And do you give a range to dial it back? Yeah, yeah, absolutely. So what I like to do is, um, I like to, yeah, exactly that. I like to use ranges. So pretty much, um, after, you know, working with the clients a little bit, a little bit of data, I set like, you know, a low end and high end, meaning like, hey, no matter what, unless something crazy... Happens this should be the number you're able to hit around this RPE threshold on the lower end, and no matter how good you're feeling, I don't want you to go higher than this. So, that's one thing I like to do. Something else that I like to do sometimes is assign loads to people, and with those assigned loads, have them engage. Hey, what do you think dispels our RPEs? You know, with their accessory work, I have them track their RPEs as well. And that's the tool that I've found works really, really well. It's like just giving them assigned loads and having them do that consistently while kind of engaging with the RPEs. As you get better at that, you can kind of give them more free reign with that. And even then, no matter... What I even like about most advanced selectors is that I love using ranges when it comes to the RPE. It's just that little bit of insurance that they're not going to go beyond kind of where they should be from an objective load perspective. Yep. To go along, I'll say one thing before is that I love ranges; I use them with most everyone. But there are actually, I don't know if you all have some athletes, but I do have some athletes that don't like to be constrained. However, they are very, very good with their RPEs. They like to have a little bit more control over their decisions. Even though it's probably in the same range I give, they just don't like being constrained. So, some athletes don't give that for the reason that they actually like to feel. Like, they have a little bit more control over their training, and since they are very responsible within it, I don't give them ranges. I just kind of give them an RPE and let them go with it. But within that too, one, it could be percentage-based in the first couple of weeks of a block to RPEs later in the block. That's one thing. It could be RPE top sets and percentage-based back downs. I think that was what you were partially alluding to, Marcellus. But the thing I'll kind of add is that overshooting's not bad. That can be a good trait for some people because undershooting is just as bad as overshooting, and you have people who are chronic undershooters too. So I think on a lifter psychology way, if I have someone who's just a chronic... Overshooters, I have to understand why, and it's because, in some manner, their reward system—that is what they feel— they feel rewarded from being able to push to a certain intensity and, like, being able to really kind of force things. So, it's setting up expectations of the block for them. Maybe those lifters, I'm pushing to RPE 9 more so at the end of the block because I know if I don't do that, they're gonna feel like they just had something there and they didn't really get that reward from the block. So, there's someone I'm going to set up a little bit longer progression model on the block to know. I'm going to start out lighter, and we're gonna make bigger jumps because we're going to push RPE 9 by the end of the block. That's also someone I'm going to be, probably, very explanatory—like a block overview of what we're trying to accomplish on certain days. I'll let them know, 'Hey, this is the day, and these are the weeks I want you to go hard on this exact set. This is the day that I need you to hold back for me.' If you do that for me, I promise I'm going to unleash you here. I'll let them know when they're going to get that reward, and if they do, you usually won't have too much of an issue.
